items.passage:
Every time a person opens a free app, a bargain is struck, though neither side states its terms plainly. The user gets a service that would cost money to build and run, and the company gets data: location, contacts, browsing history, and the pattern of taps and pauses that reveals what holds attention. The user is told that consent has been given, because a box was ticked on a screen that appeared before the service could be used. Both sides then proceed as if a genuine agreement had been reached, when what actually happened was closer to a toll: pay with your data, or do not pass. The question is whether a tick given under those conditions can count as consent at all.
The defenders of the current system argue that users do understand the bargain and accept it. People know, they say, that free services are paid for with advertising, and advertising needs data. If users truly objected, they would stop using the services, and they do not. The fact that billions of people continue to use these apps is, on this view, evidence that the bargain is acceptable.  But knowing in general terms is not the same as knowing what is collected, who it is sold to, and what inferences are drawn from it. 
The law has tried to close this gap by requiring consent to be specific, informed and freely given. In practice, the requirement has produced consent screens of remarkable length and obscurity, written in legal language that few readers finish and fewer understand. Companies comply with the letter of the law by disclosing everything, and defeat its purpose by disclosing it in a form nobody can use. The result is consent fatigue: users click accept on everything, not because they agree, but because refusing means losing the service and reading the policy means losing the afternoon. 
There are better designs, and some are already in use. One is to make the default the most private setting, so that sharing requires an active choice rather than a failure to opt out. Another is to require consent separately for each purpose, so that agreeing to location for navigation does not also agree to location for advertising. A third is to limit how long data may be kept and to require its deletion on request, with the deletion verified rather than merely promised. Each of these shifts the burden from the user, who must currently defend her privacy against a system designed to erode it, to the company, which must justify each collection. None of them destroys the business model: advertising can work with less data, as the history of advertising before the internet shows, though it works less profitably.
The deeper issue is that data is not like money. Money spent is gone, but data given can be copied endlessly, combined with other data, and used years later for purposes nobody imagined when it was collected. Consent given today cannot sensibly cover uses invented tomorrow. That is why the strongest protection is not a better consent form but a limit on collection itself: collect only what the service needs, keep it only as long as it is needed, and do not sell it at all. Until the law draws that line, the tick box will remain what it is now: a ritual that protects the company far more than the user.

items.passage:
The shift from petrol cars to electric vehicles is usually described as a technology story: batteries got cheaper, ranges got longer, and charging got faster. The technology story is true, but it is not the whole story, and in India it may not even be the main story. The main story is infrastructure, and infrastructure is a coordination problem. A buyer will not buy an electric car without chargers nearby, and nobody will build chargers without electric cars nearby to use them. Each side waits for the other, and the market stays small. Governments break this circle by subsidising one side or the other, but subsidies are expensive, and they create their own problems: chargers built where they are not needed, and cars bought by people who would have bought them anyway.
The second part of the story is the grid. An electric car is, in effect, a large battery on wheels, and a city full of them is a large new demand on the electricity system. If most owners charge in the evening, when they return home, the evening peak grows sharply, and the grid must be strengthened at great cost. If owners can be persuaded to charge at night, when demand is low, the same cars become an asset, soaking up surplus power and even, in principle, feeding it back. The difference between these two futures is not technology but pricing and habit: charge more in the evening and less at night, and behaviour follows. Few Indian cities have yet put such pricing in place, and fewer still have explained it to consumers in a way that changes when they plug in.
The third part is the supply chain. A petrol car has an engine with hundreds of moving parts, made by a network of suppliers built over decades. An electric car has a battery, a motor and electronics, and the battery is the expensive part, dominated by a small number of countries that control the minerals and the processing. For India, which imports almost all of its oil, swapping dependence on oil exporters for dependence on battery exporters is an improvement but not an escape. The government's answer has been to subsidise battery manufacturing at home, but building that capacity takes years, and the technology changes while it is being built. A factory designed for one battery chemistry can be outdated before it opens.
None of this means the transition will fail. Electric two-wheelers, which need smaller batteries and shorter ranges, are already selling in large numbers, and they suit Indian cities, where most trips are short. Buses and three-wheelers, which run fixed routes and return to a depot every night, are even easier to electrify, and several cities have already begun. The passenger car, the vehicle the debate focuses on, is the hardest case, because it needs long range, fast charging and a large battery. The sensible sequence is therefore to electrify first where it is easiest, learn from those fleets, and let the car follow. A transition that starts with buses and scooters and ends with cars is less dramatic than one that starts with cars, but it is far more likely to arrive.
